chunks: Why step-down regulators dominate. The question: In many embedded systems, why are step-down regulators more common than step-up regulators?
Most power rails inside a device are stepped down from a higher voltage, because the sources are usually higher than what the chips need.
Chip voltages keep falling, since lower voltage saves a lot of power. Moving power at high voltage and converting down near the load also wastes less in the wires.
Think of a water tower on a hill. It is easy to let water run down to many houses and lower its pressure with valves at each tap. Pushing water uphill needs a pump and extra work.
Electronics is similar: getting from a high voltage down to a low one is the natural, simple direction.
Almost every arrow is a step-down. The one place a step-up would appear is when a battery replaces the adapter and sags below the 3. 3 volts or 5 volts rail.
Step-down: output voltage lower than input. Rail: a supply line at a particular voltage. I to the 2R loss: heat in a wire, which grows with the square of the current.
Chip switching power: the power chips use to flip their tiny switches. It scales with V squared , so lower voltage means much lower power.
Boost converter: a step-up converter, harder to design than a buck.
A 10 watts load at 1 volts draws 10 amps. At 12 volts, the same power needs only about 0. 83 amps. Through a trace of 10 milliohms, the 10 amps case loses 10 squared times 0.
01 equals 1 watts, while the 0. 83 amps case loses about 0. 007 watts. So bring the power in at 12 volts and convert down right next to the load. That is the whole idea.
"Because supplies are usually higher than what the chips need, and chips keep going lower in voltage to save CV-squared-f power.
Distributing at a higher voltage also means less current and less I-squared-R loss, so you convert down at the point of load.
Step-down converters are also simpler: a buck has continuous output current and no right-half-plane zero, while a boost has higher input current, a pulsed output and no short-circuit isolation.
Step-up shows up when a battery dips below the rail."
